idiom_name: recipient list (distribution or auction broadcast) + correlation identifier + aggregator with an explicit completeness condition
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form of the EIP structure: resolve the recipient set (a data-driven Recipient List for the distribution variant, a Publish-Subscribe Channel for the auction variant), give every request a correlation identifier and a return address, issue the requests concurrently, and let one aggregator key the replies by that identifier. The aggregator's completeness condition must be stated explicitly - wait for all, first acceptable, k-of-n, or a fixed time budget - plus the rule for partial results. Reap the stragglers (cancel, drain or expire) so late replies cannot re-enter the aggregation, and keep the per-request state TTL-bounded.
code_sketch:
request = correlate(payload, new_id())
responses = []
for r in recipients(resolve(request)):        # distribution (list) or auction (pub-sub)
    channel(r).send(request)                  # concurrently
while not complete(responses, policy):        # all | first_ok | k_of_n | deadline
    responses += inbox.collect(request.id, budget_remaining())
merge(responses)                              # report which recipients answered
pitfalls: Leaving the completeness condition implicit: the gather then either waits forever or returns a partial answer that looks complete.
No reaping of losers: cancelled requests keep consuming resources and late replies re-enter an aggregation that has already answered.
Broadcasting a side-effecting command: the fan-out multiplies the effect by the recipient count unless the responders are Idempotent Receivers.
Per-request correlation state without a TTL leaks memory in long-lived aggregators.

Wrong move: aggregating with an all-or-nothing combinator -> one failed recipient discards every reply that already arrived (Spring Integration warns that an exception thrown from one sub-flow is re-thrown upstream so the other sub-flows 'work for nothing') -> collect per-recipient settled results (gather with return_exceptions, per-future error handling, a Camel AggregationStrategy timeout callback) and merge the survivors.

Wrong move: reusing a coarse or cached correlation key across requests -> replies from two in-flight gathers merge into one group and the answer mixes providers -> mint a fresh unique correlation identifier per scatter and attribute or discard every reply by it.

Wrong move: merging replies in arrival order -> a fast but stale replica or degraded provider overwrites the authoritative answer -> stamp each reply with a version or freshness marker and let the merge policy rank on that, the way an Elasticsearch coordinator reduces shard results by sort values rather than by who answered first.
